network.overall_strategy: Construct a connected terrestrial network containing 10 distinct feedstock or activation sequences. These are not 10 independently demonstrated environmental syntheses: three pathways are alternative implementations of lactaldehyde photochemistry, two converge through glycine, and four represent experimentally supported but mechanistically unresolved reaction ensembles. The strongest defined target-forming branches are aminomalononitrile plus acetaldehyde and glycine plus acetaldehyde. Photoredox chemistry has strong precursor-level support, but environmentally effective aminonitrile hydrolysis remains unverified. The target node denotes racemic threo-threonine, not enantiopure L-threonine; racemic allo-threonine is represented separately where supported. Stereochemistry-unspecified intermediates denote defined constitutions with unresolved stereoisomers. All conditions explicitly identified as proposed are test conditions, not reported experimental results. Ensemble reactions include precursor production and subsequent hydrolysis without inventing molecular identities for unidentified residues. Their listed coproducts provide formal material-balance closure, not measured product allocations; automatically inferred coefficients must not be interpreted as yields or stereoisomer ratios. Neutral molecular formulas generally represent acid-base families under the stated pH. Terminal coproducts use the schema's intermediate role because no byproduct role is available. All pathways are anoxic. No hot-vent synthesis or cryogenic extraterrestrial experiment is relabeled as a demonstrated terrestrial surface reaction.

reactions.name: Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Approximately neutral to mildly alkaline water; proposed pH 7-9 and millimolar-to-tens-of-millimolar reactants. Retain volatile HCN and acetaldehyde through gas-water equilibration. Addition is reversible; no quantitative environmental conversion is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the acetaldehyde carbonyl and proton transfer gives lactonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the experimentally grounded entry to the lactaldehyde branch in Ritson and Sutherland (2013), incorporated into Patel et al. (2015). No mineral catalyst is required. Concentration, volatilization and competing cyanide oligomerization constrain flux; alkaline-lake cyanide storage provides a possible supply mechanism but does not establish simultaneous reagent availability (Toner and Catling, 2019).

reactions.name: Copper-assisted sulfidic photoreduction of lactonitrile
agents: Copper(I) cyanide, CuCN, as a photoredox component

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with a sulfide-retaining headspace
conditions.catalyst: CuCN, approximately 10 mol% relative to nitrile
conditions.other: Approximately pH 7; 254 nm irradiation; 2 h reference exposure. A starting test formulation is 10 mM lactonitrile, 30 mM total sulfide, 33 mM phosphate and 1 mM CuCN. These concentrations are transferred from the study's representative nitrile experiment, not asserted to reproduce its exact lactaldehyde experiment. Measure UV transmission and dissolved catalyst speciation.

reactions.mechanism: Photogenerated reducing equivalents reduce the nitrile to an imine-level intermediate; hydrolysis releases lactaldehyde and ammonia. Sulfide supplies reducing equivalents. Elemental sulfur represents the oxidized sulfur pool, whose actual speciation may include polysulfides.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland (2013) reported lactaldehyde in 19% yield after 2 h from the acetaldehyde-cyanohydrin system. That measured yield is not assigned to the proposed formulation above. Copper accelerates the demonstrated implementation, but sulfide precipitation, catalyst speciation and UV attenuation must be resolved in a natural setting (Patel et al., 2015; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Candidate copper-free sulfidic photoreduction

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with a sulfide-retaining headspace
conditions.other: Proposed matched comparison with rxn_002: pH 7, 10 mM lactonitrile, 30 mM total sulfide, 33 mM phosphate, 254 nm irradiation and 2-24 h sampling, but no added copper. This exposure range is a test design, not a reported productive operating window.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide-derived photochemical reducing equivalents are proposed to reduce the nitrile, followed by imine hydrolysis. Elemental sulfur is a formal oxidized-sulfur endpoint rather than a measured exclusive product.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this substrate-specific implementation. Patel et al. (2015) support copper-independent reduction in parts of sulfidic photochemistry, but the supplied evidence does not establish copper-free lactonitrile-to-lactaldehyde yield or selectivity. This alternative tests a genuine catalyst-availability constraint rather than assuming copper is universally necessary. Sulfide supply and UV compatibility remain unresolved (Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Candidate ferrocyanide-sulfite photoreduction
agents: Ferrocyanide, [Fe(CN)6]4-, as a photoelectron donor and photoredox component

conditions.other: Proposed substrate test: 10 mM lactonitrile, 30-100 mM total sulfite/bisulfite, pH 7-8, 254 nm irradiation and 2-24 h sampling. These values are not reported lactonitrile conditions. Quantify ferrocyanide/ferricyanide turnover, cyanide loss, sulfate formation and competing sulfur products. No oxygen is required or supplied.

reactions.mechanism: Photoelectron release from ferrocyanide is proposed to drive nitrile reduction; sulfite supplies net reducing equivalents while supporting photoredox turnover. Imine hydrolysis gives lactaldehyde. Sulfate is a formal fully oxidized donor endpoint.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate extension. Xu et al. (2018) demonstrated sulfite/ferrocyanide-driven HCN reductive homologation, not this lactonitrile-to-threonine sequence. The alternative has geochemical merit because sulfite can be more accessible than sulfide, but neither catalyst turnover nor substrate selectivity follows from a balanced equation (Ranjan et al., 2018). Ferrocyanide accumulation is plausible in some alkaline lakes, not universal (Toner and Catling, 2019).

reactions.name: Lactaldehyde cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Approximately neutral to mildly alkaline water. Proposed starting concentrations are 1-10 mM lactaldehyde with cyanide at comparable concentration or modest excess. Preserve the aldehyde against competing reduction, condensation and decomposition; treat cyanohydrin formation as an equilibrium.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide addition to lactaldehyde gives 2,3-dihydroxybutanenitrile, introducing the carbon that can become threonine's carboxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland (2013) described conversion of lactaldehyde through its cyanohydrin into the threonine/allothreonine aminonitrile. Resolving this intermediate avoids treating Strecker chemistry as instantaneous. Lactaldehyde lifetime in realistic mixed solutions is an unmeasured bottleneck.

reactions.name: Ammonia-dependent conversion to the threonine aminonitrile

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with ammonia-retaining gas-water contact
conditions.other: Excess ammonia; proposed total ammonia approximately 0.1 M with 1-10 mM cyanohydrin and pH 8-9. Monitor for days to weeks. Ammonia addition and pH adjustment follow photoreduction rather than assuming all stages share one optimized solution.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanohydrin dissociation, carbonyl-imine equilibration and cyanide trapping produce the alpha-aminonitrile. This is not modeled as direct displacement of an unactivated hydroxyl group by ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: The threonine/allothreonine aminonitrile endpoint is supported by Ritson and Sutherland (2013). Related conversions required days to weeks. The proposed concentration bracket is not a published optimum, and no stereochemical enrichment or quantitative conversion is assumed.

reactions.name: Aminonitrile hydration to a threoninamide intermediate
agents: Hydronium ions for general acid catalysis

conditions.other: A distinct acidic, warmed stage is required after ammonia-rich Strecker chemistry. Proposed monitoring spans days to months; this is not a known conversion time. Measure aminonitrile loss, amide formation and competing decomposition separately.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile protonation and water addition produce an imidic intermediate that tautomerizes to the primary amide.
reactions.reasoning: This is an inferred standard nitrile-hydrolysis intermediate, not a threoninamide isolated in the supplied threonine experiment. Ritson and Sutherland (2013) establish the aminonitrile, not environmentally effective free-threonine production. The stated mild mineral-acid implementation is speculative and is retained because hydrolysis is chemically necessary, not because its environmental kinetics are known.

reactions.name: Threoninamide hydrolysis to free threonine-family amino acids
agents: Hydronium ions for general acid catalysis

conditions.other: Continue the separate acidic hydrolysis stage and measure free amino-acid accumulation against degradation over days to months. Ammonia is predominantly ammonium at this pH. Neither complete hydrolysis nor a threonine:allothreonine ratio is assigned.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed amide hydrolysis forms the carboxylic acid and releases ammonia/ammonium while retaining the precursor carbon skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Chemically standard completion of a Strecker route, but environmentally productive rates are speculative here. Strong analytical hydrolysis in historical cyanide studies cannot establish conversion at pH 1-2 and 350-370 K (Matthews and Moser, 1967; Draganić et al., 1977). Ritson and Sutherland (2013) did not establish an isolated free-threonine yield for this proposed environmental completion.

reactions.name: HCN oligomerization to aminomalononitrile

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with minimized HCN escape
conditions.other: Concentrated cyanide solution; proposed screening bracket 0.1-1 M total HCN/cyanide, pH 9-10 and aging over days to weeks. Quantify aminomalononitrile rather than equating total polymer formation with useful trimer yield. These are proposed bounds, not source-specific measured conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide-initiated HCN oligomerization generates the trimer aminomalononitrile, which competes with further oligomerization and hydrolysis.
reactions.reasoning: Aminomalononitrile is the established HCN trimer used by Thanassi (1975); broader cyanide oligomerization is supported by Lowe et al. (1963). Selective accumulation is not demonstrated by bulk-polymer production. Cyanide concentration and retention require a localized reservoir, potentially involving the storage processes examined by Toner and Catling (2019).

reactions.name: Aminomalononitrile addition to acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Approximately neutral solution. Proposed pH 6.5-7.5 and millimolar-to-tens-of-millimolar reactants, with an hours-to-days sampling series. The supplied literature summary does not provide an exact concentration, residence time or threonine yield.

reactions.mechanism: The activated central carbon of aminomalononitrile forms a carbon-carbon bond with acetaldehyde, generating a hydroxyethyl-substituted dinitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Thanassi (1975) demonstrated threonine and allothreonine after acetaldehyde reaction followed by hydrolysis/decarboxylation; Kuroda et al. (2020) describe the addition as occurring in nearly neutral water. No mineral catalyst is justified. The adduct is a mechanistic representation of the productive connectivity, not an assertion that every intermediate was isolated.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of the hydroxyethyl-substituted dinitrile
agents: Hydronium ions for acid-catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis

conditions.other: Separate hydrolysis stage after near-neutral carbon-carbon bond formation. Follow both nitriles through partially hydrolyzed products over days to months. Thanassi's acid-workup endpoint supports the chemistry, but the supplied summary does not establish rates under this milder proposed regime.

reactions.mechanism: Successive hydration and hydrolysis of both nitriles gives the substituted aminomalonic acid and ammonia/ammonium. The reaction node lumps the individual amide-hydrolysis events.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis/decarboxylation is supported at the net experimental level by Thanassi (1975), as discussed by Kuroda et al. (2020). The explicitly drawn dicarboxylic acid is mechanistically inferred. Free-threonine accumulation under realistic acidic-pool conditions remains speculative; a successful strong-acid workup does not supply those kinetics.

reactions.name: Decarboxylation to threonine and allothreonine

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with carbon dioxide escape
conditions.other: Acidic to weakly acidic water, proposed pH 2-5. Decarboxylation may overlap the preceding hydrolysis rather than requiring isolation of the diacid. Determine its rate and stereoisomer distribution experimentally.

reactions.mechanism: Loss of one carboxyl group from the substituted aminomalonic acid, followed by protonation, creates the alpha-amino-acid center and releases carbon dioxide.
reactions.reasoning: Thanassi (1975) directly supports D,L-threonine and allothreonine after the combined addition/hydrolysis/decarboxylation sequence. The mechanism is consistent with an aminomalonate intermediate, but the supplied evidence does not establish the isolated rate or selectivity of this individual step. No enantioselection is claimed.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde Strecker synthesis of aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed pH 8-9, formaldehyde and cyanide at millimolar-to-tens-of-millimolar concentrations, and ammonia in excess. Sample over hours to days. Preserve volatile reactants and quantify competing cyanohydrin, imine and oligomer pools.

reactions.mechanism: Formaldehyde-ammonia imine chemistry followed by cyanide addition produces aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is an established Strecker reaction class used here as a glycine-supply module, not a threonine synthesis demonstrated in the supplied papers. Its integration under the stated surface conditions is speculative. The mechanistic analogy is supported by the aminonitrile chemistry of Ritson and Sutherland (2013); the downstream reason to make glycine is the experimentally observed aldehyde-amino-acid chemistry of Ivanov and Ivanov (1983).

reactions.name: Aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis to glycine

conditions.other: A separate acidic stage follows aminoacetonitrile formation. Monitor nitrile, glycinamide and glycine over days to months; no environmental rate or completion fraction is assigned. Subsequently adjust to the weaker acidity required by rxn_015.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis convert aminoacetonitrile to glycine while releasing ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: Standard Strecker completion supplies the glycine required by Ivanov and Ivanov (1983). The specific environmental operating window is speculative rather than established by that study. Cyanide-derived amino-acid recovery after hydrolysis supports chemical accessibility, not quantitative conversion under the proposed mild workup (Lowe et al., 1963; Draganić et al., 1977).

reactions.name: Glycine-acetaldehyde carbon-carbon bond formation

conditions.other: pH 3.3-3.7; homogeneous weakly acidic water with no inorganic solids. Glycine and acetaldehyde must coexist at useful concentrations. Exact reactant concentrations and residence times are not supplied in the research summary and are not invented here. Allothreonine is a possible stereochemical coproduct; its yield was not reported.

reactions.mechanism: The observed aldehyde-amino-acid reaction network forms the required bond between glycine's alpha carbon and acetaldehyde's carbonyl carbon. The net connectivity is aldol-like, but a free glycine enolate under acidic conditions is not assumed to be the established microscopic mechanism.
reactions.reasoning: Ivanov and Ivanov (1983) detected threonine in glycine/oligoglycine-aldehyde experiments at these temperatures and pH without inorganic solids. This edge represents the productive branch of a broad reaction network, not a selective binary synthesis with known yield. Generic aldehyde-ammonia chemistry cannot substitute for this evidence: Koga and Naraoka (2017) did not convincingly produce threonine in their different aldehyde system.

reactions.name: Alternative glycine supply through aminomalononitrile hydrolysis
agents: Hydronium ions for acid-catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis

conditions.other: Hydrolyze an aminomalononitrile-bearing fraction before introducing acetaldehyde. Monitor nitrile disappearance, partial hydrolysis products and decarboxylation over days to months. This branch competes with rxn_010 rather than presuming both consume the same material quantitatively.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the two nitrile groups forms aminomalonic acid and releases ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as an explicitly resolved environmental supply branch in this network. The chemistry follows ordinary dinitrile hydrolysis and the aminomalononitrile framework of Thanassi (1975), but the supplied research does not independently establish this isolated intermediate under the proposed conditions. It is chemically motivated because it supplies glycine without requiring a formaldehyde feed.

reactions.name: Aminomalonic acid decarboxylation to glycine

conditions.other: Acidic to weakly acidic water; carbon dioxide can escape. Decarboxylation may occur during rxn_016. Measure glycine recovery before adjusting to pH 3.3-3.7 and adding acetaldehyde.

reactions.mechanism: Aminomalonic acid loses carbon dioxide; protonation gives glycine.
reactions.reasoning: This is chemically expected aminomalonate decarboxylation, but its environmental kinetics and coupling to rxn_015 are speculative in the supplied evidence. It is an unsubstituted counterpart of the hydrolysis/decarboxylation logic associated with Thanassi (1975). Ivanov and Ivanov (1983) support the subsequent glycine-dependent target-forming step, not this integrated upstream sequence.

reactions.name: Thermal HCN-ammonia reaction ensemble followed by hydrolysis
agents: Hydronium ions during the subsequent hydrolysis stage

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K proposed aging stage; 350-370 K candidate environmental hydrolysis
conditions.other: Proposed aging bracket: 0.1-1 M total cyanide, ammoniacal pH 9-10, days to weeks. These are screening conditions, not reconstructed historical values. Historical evidence relies on strong acid hydrolysis, including approximately 6 N HCl near 373 K for many hours. Replacing that workup with pH 1-2 at 350-370 K is an unvalidated environmental extension.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved HCN oligomerization and subsequent water/ammonia chemistry generate hydrolyzable material containing threonine precursors. Later hydrolysis releases threonine. Ammonia and carbon dioxide are formal coproduct pools, not a demonstrated exclusive product distribution.
reactions.reasoning: Lowe et al. (1963) and Matthews and Moser (1966, 1967) support complex cyanide-derived products and threonine in hydrolysates. The immediate precursor is unidentified, so no fictitious polymer molecule is assigned. This establishes laboratory precursor accessibility, not free-threonine accumulation during aging. Cyanide concentration and environmentally adequate hydrolysis remain separate unresolved requirements.

reactions.name: Gamma-radiolysis of aqueous cyanide followed by hydrolysis
agents: Hydronium ions during the subsequent hydrolysis stage

conditions.temperature: Approximately 300 K irradiation analogue; 350-370 K candidate environmental hydrolysis
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm, oxygen-free and sealed against HCN loss
conditions.catalyst: No irradiation catalyst; acid catalysis during hydrolysis
conditions.other: Experimentally reported HCN concentration: 0.004-0.1 M. Laboratory activation: cobalt-60 gamma radiation at approximately 2 kGy/h. The supplied summary does not specify total dose or all hydrolysis parameters. No natural terrestrial dose rate or irradiation duration is assigned. A pH 1-2 environmental hydrolysis replacement is hypothetical.

reactions.mechanism: Water- and cyanide-derived radicals form an unresolved oligomeric precursor inventory; subsequent hydrolysis releases threonine. Hydrogen represents a possible radiolytic reducing-product pool, while carbon dioxide and ammonia provide formal balance closure rather than measured threonine-specific coproduct yields.
reactions.reasoning: Sweeney et al. (1976) and Draganić et al. (1977) support threonine recovery after irradiation and hydrolysis, with approximately racemic chiral products. Cobalt-60 is a laboratory proxy, not an asserted Hadean energy source. Without natural dosimetry and environmental hydrolysis kinetics, this remains a laboratory-supported ensemble with unquantified terrestrial flux.

reactions.name: H2S-rich gas-water electrical-discharge ensemble
agents: Tungsten electrode surfaces in the laboratory apparatus; any catalytic contribution is unresolved

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk-fluid analogue; discharge channels are transiently much hotter
conditions.pressure: Initial dry-gas total approximately 695 mmHg, plus water vapor
conditions.other: Reference apparatus: 5 L, CH4 258 mmHg, H2S 100 mmHg, NH3 250 mmHg and CO2 87 mmHg, with electrical discharge and gas-water recirculation. The supplied summary does not specify discharge power, duration or complete sample workup. Sulfur deposition near tungsten electrodes was observed. No natural lightning exposure equivalent is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: An unresolved gas-phase and aqueous network produces organic precursors and amino acids. The threonine-forming sequence is not assigned to a particular Strecker or radical mechanism. Hydrogen and sulfur are formal coproduct pools, not measured stoichiometric partners of threonine.
reactions.reasoning: Parker et al. (2011) detected threonine in the archived H2S-rich Miller experiment. The gas composition and possible electrode effects are specified rather than hidden under a generic surface label. This is a laboratory product-level result; an analogous natural setting would require a local or transient reducing plume, gas-water capture and sufficient discharge exposure. It does not demonstrate production in a global CO2/N2 atmosphere.

reactions.name: Dry methane-ammonia discharge followed by residue hydrolysis
agents: Hydronium ions during the later residue-hydrolysis stage

conditions.temperature: Approximately 300 K bulk dry-gas analogue; 350-370 K candidate aqueous hydrolysis
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm proposed analogue; original value not supplied
conditions.catalyst: No established discharge catalyst; acid catalysis during hydrolysis
conditions.other: The initial CH4/NH3 activation stage is dry; listed water is introduced only during subsequent residue hydrolysis. The supplied summary does not establish gas ratio, discharge energy, exposure time or residue residence time. Historical evidence uses laboratory hydrolysis; a later pH 1-2 warm-water stage is an unvalidated environmental replacement. The aqueous flag describes the initial activation stage.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical discharge produces an unresolved nitrogen-rich organic residue. Subsequent hydration and hydrolysis release threonine. Hydrogen is a formal net dehydrogenation coproduct; the equation is not an identified elementary synthesis or measured product allocation.
reactions.reasoning: Matthews and Moser (1966, 1967) support threonine in hydrolysates of discharge-generated material. This differs experimentally from the wet H2S-rich Miller ensemble, but it does not establish a naturally maintained dry methane/ammonia reservoir. Dry-stage preservation, subsequent wetting and productive environmental hydrolysis remain unquantified; these gaps are not filled with invented operating values.

pathways.name: Copper-assisted lactaldehyde-Strecker route
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde undergoes cyanohydrin formation and demonstrated copper-assisted photoreductive homologation. Lactaldehyde then reaches the experimentally supported threonine aminonitrile. The final two hydrolysis steps are chemically justified but environmentally unvalidated bottlenecks.

pathways.name: Copper-free sulfidic implementation
pathways.description: An activation-distinct alternative to P1 that removes the copper requirement. It is a substrate-specific hypothesis, not an independently demonstrated lactonitrile-to-threonine synthesis. Productive copper-free reduction and subsequent environmental hydrolysis both require validation.

pathways.name: Sulfite-ferrocyanide implementation
pathways.description: Tests a different reductant and photoredox component to address sulfide-availability constraints. General homologation has experimental support, but the lactonitrile-specific reduction, catalyst turnover and free-threonine completion are not demonstrated by the supplied study.

pathways.name: Aminomalononitrile-acetaldehyde route
pathways.description: HCN trimerization supplies an activated carbon nucleophile. Acetaldehyde addition followed by hydrolysis and decarboxylation accesses threonine and allothreonine. The target endpoint is experimentally supported after acid workup; precursor accumulation and a milder environmental workup are not established.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde-Strecker glycine supply followed by acetaldehyde coupling
pathways.description: A conventional aminoacetonitrile route supplies glycine, which enters the experimentally observed warm, weakly acidic aldehyde-amino-acid chemistry. The target-forming step requires no mineral catalyst, but integrated glycine production, pH staging and product yields remain unmeasured.

pathways.name: HCN-trimer-derived glycine followed by acetaldehyde coupling
pathways.description: Aminomalononitrile is hydrolyzed and decarboxylated before acetaldehyde addition, unlike P4 where carbon-carbon bond formation precedes hydrolysis. This avoids a formaldehyde feed but is an inferred integrated supply route, not a demonstrated complete environmental synthesis.

pathways.name: Thermal ammoniacal HCN ensemble
pathways.description: Concentrated cyanide chemistry generates unidentified hydrolyzable precursors from which threonine has been recovered. The single reaction node explicitly lumps precursor formation and later hydrolysis; it does not assert that free threonine forms during polymer aging.

pathways.name: Ionizing-radiation cyanide ensemble
pathways.description: Aqueous cyanide irradiation followed by hydrolysis has a direct experimental threonine endpoint. The precursor sequence is unresolved, and no natural dose rate, required accumulation time or mild environmental hydrolysis efficiency is established.

pathways.name: H2S-rich gas-water discharge ensemble
pathways.description: Represents the threonine-positive Miller configuration with explicit reference gas partial pressures and possible electrode effects. Its natural analogue requires local reducing conditions and effective gas-water cycling; a particular molecular mechanism is not inferred from product detection.

pathways.name: Dry reducing-gas discharge and subsequent hydrolysis
pathways.description: Separates dry energetic residue formation from later water-dependent release of threonine. Historical laboratory recovery supports accessibility, while gas maintenance, residue survival, exposure and environmentally effective hydrolysis remain open.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The defined carbon-skeleton chemistry closely follows Ritson and Sutherland (2013), including experimentally supported lactaldehyde and threonine-family aminonitrile formation. The network correctly acknowledges that this is principally precursor-level evidence. Hydration and amide hydrolysis are chemically credible, but their rates and product recovery under an assigned surface regime remain unspecified. Copper-assisted photochemistry also requires a demonstrated balance between available reductant, copper speciation and UV penetration.
suggestions: Specify pH, temperature, concentrations and residence times for aminonitrile formation, hydration and amide hydrolysis; measure free threonine recovery and competing losses.
Specify Cu(I) loading and speciation, sulfide supply, irradiation spectrum and fluence, and optical depth; assess metal-sulfide precipitation.
Keep the experimentally established aminonitrile endpoint distinct from the proposed environmental completion to free amino acids.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Copper-free sulfidic photoreduction has relevant support in the broader cyanosulfidic literature, including Patel et al. (2015), but that does not establish lactonitrile-to-lactaldehyde performance under this pathway's unspecified conditions. Calling rxn_003 a candidate is appropriate. The subsequent Strecker connectivity is sound, while the same environmentally unverified hydrolysis steps as P1 limit target completion.
suggestions: Demonstrate substrate-specific copper-free lactonitrile reduction, with lactaldehyde identification, absolute yield and competing-product measurements.
Quantify sulfide availability and UV transmission under the selected surface conditions rather than assuming that removing copper resolves all environmental constraints.
Validate aminonitrile-to-free-threonine conversion under explicitly assigned hydrolysis conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Xu et al. (2018) support sulfite-ferrocyanide photoredox homologation, making rxn_004 a reasonable, explicitly labeled extrapolation. The supplied research does not establish this specific lactonitrile conversion or a threonine endpoint using that implementation. The deterministic check establishes conservation for the sulfite-to-sulfate equation, but not catalytic turnover or product selectivity. Ferrocyanide availability and downstream hydrolysis remain unparameterized.
suggestions: Measure lactaldehyde formation from lactonitrile in the sulfite-ferrocyanide system rather than transferring yields from other substrates.
Include ferrocyanide in the environmental catalyst inventory and specify its concentration, stability, irradiation conditions and reductant budget.
Establish free-threonine recovery through the proposed hydration and hydrolysis sequence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest chemically defined target-forming branch. Thanassi (1975), also discussed by Kuroda et al. (2020), directly supports aminomalononitrile-acetaldehyde chemistry followed by hydrolysis/decarboxylation yielding threonine and allo-threonine. The proposed intermediates have appropriate constitutions and formulas. The principal limitations are obtaining and retaining aminomalononitrile from competing HCN oligomerization chemistry and justifying the acid-hydrolysis stage environmentally; the laboratory endpoint does not by itself establish that surface implementation.
suggestions: Specify HCN concentration, pH, reaction time and aminomalononitrile recovery, including losses to other oligomers.
Assign an acid source, acidity, temperature and duration for hydrolysis; test weaker environmental alternatives rather than assuming equivalence to laboratory workup.
Quantify overall threonine recovery, stereoisomer distribution and product survival through hydrolysis/decarboxylation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Formaldehyde Strecker chemistry provides a credible glycine supply. Ivanov and Ivanov (1983) support threonine formation from glycine/oligoglycine and acetaldehyde at pH 3.3–3.7 and 60–80 °C without inorganic solids. This supports rxn_015 as a net product-forming channel, not a selective elementary reaction. The submitted network does not actually assign those conditions, quantify competing chemistry, or establish glycine recovery through rxn_014. The explicit allo-threonine output warrants stereoisomer-specific verification.
suggestions: Specify aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis conditions and the resulting glycine concentration and recovery.
Parameterize rxn_015 using the reported weakly acidic, warm aqueous regime, including substrate concentrations and reaction duration.
Measure absolute threonine yield and stereoisomer-resolved products; retain allo-threonine as an uncertain output unless directly supported.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Aminomalononitrile hydrolysis to aminomalonic acid followed by decarboxylation is a chemically credible glycine supply, and the terminal glycine-acetaldehyde channel has experimental support from Ivanov and Ivanov (1983). Compared with P5, this implementation has less established precursor availability and integrated recovery. HCN oligomerization, dinitrile hydrolysis and warm weak-acid coupling require explicit operating regimes and material continuity, although they need not occur in one vessel or one unchanged environment.
suggestions: Measure glycine recovery through aminomalononitrile hydrolysis and aminomalonic-acid decarboxylation under stated conditions.
Specify concentration and pH changes, dilution and intermediate losses between the precursor-production and acetaldehyde-coupling stages.
Quantify the mixed-product outcome of rxn_015 and verify its stereoisomer assignments.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Matthews and Moser studies support threonine recovered after hydrolysis of HCN-derived material. Representing this as an unresolved ensemble is appropriate and avoids inventing precursor identities. However, rxn_018 includes both precursor production and hydrolysis, so the evidence does not establish free threonine accumulation in an unspecified thermal surface pool. Required cyanide concentrations, heating conditions, hydrolysis severity and environmental sources of those conditions are not supplied.
suggestions: Retain the ensemble representation but separately annotate precursor-generation and hydrolysis conditions, durations and measured recoveries.
Provide a physically supported cyanide concentration and retention mechanism for the selected setting.
Distinguish free threonine before hydrolysis from hydrolyzable threonine equivalents and quantify both.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Sweeney et al. (1976) and Draganić et al. (1977) provide direct evidence for threonine recovered after irradiation and hydrolysis of aqueous cyanide. The ensemble treatment matches the unresolved oligomer chemistry. The largest environmental gap is dosimetry: the approximately 2 kGy/h laboratory irradiation does not identify a natural surface exposure capable of useful net production. Subsequent hydrolysis and competition between radiation-driven synthesis and destruction also remain unspecified.
suggestions: Specify a plausible natural radiation source, dose rate, integrated dose, exposure geometry and residence time.
Evaluate production and degradation together at the modeled environmental dose rate; a natural source need not reproduce the laboratory rate if net accumulation is demonstrated.
Assign hydrolysis conditions and measure free versus hydrolysis-released threonine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Parker et al. (2011) provide strong target-level evidence from the H2S-rich gas-water discharge experiment, and an ensemble edge is appropriate because the threonine-forming mechanism is unresolved. The network does not falsely claim a resolved elementary pathway. Nevertheless, 'Surface' does not establish the required local gas composition, discharge exposure, collection efficiency or workup. Possible tungsten-electrode/sulfur effects are an experimental uncertainty, not evidence that tungsten is necessarily required.
suggestions: Specify gas partial pressures, water temperature, discharge energy and duration, circulation and product-collection conditions.
Justify the selected reducing gas inventory in a local or transient setting rather than assuming its environmental availability.
Test sensitivity to electrode and sulfur-surface chemistry, and distinguish reactor products from products released during workup.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Matthews and Moser (1966) support threonine released by hydrolysis of residues generated in dry methane-ammonia discharge experiments. Including water in the overall equation is legitimate because the network explicitly assigns it to subsequent hydrolysis, not the dry discharge stage. The unresolved issues are environmental maintenance of the dry reducing gas mixture, residue collection and wetting, and hydrolysis sufficient to release free threonine.
suggestions: Annotate the dry discharge, residue collection and aqueous hydrolysis as distinct stages within the ensemble.
Provide a physical setting and transport mechanism connecting residue formation to hydrolysis without assuming quantitative collection.
Measure absolute free-threonine recovery and product losses under environmentally justified hydrolysis conditions.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally sound: its 25 molecule nodes and 21 reaction nodes form a connected graph, molecule IDs are consistent, and the deterministic check establishes zero conservation violations. Inferred coefficients, including sulfur multiples and coefficients for stereoisomer mixtures, are not yields or stereoisomer ratios. Listed problematic reactions concern evidence or environmental implementation, not atom or charge balance. Literature alignment is substantively strong: precursor-only photochemistry, candidate photoredox alternatives, demonstrated target-forming branches and unresolved ensembles are appropriately distinguished. Racemic threo-threonine satisfies the stated target; lack of L-enantiopurity is not a defect. P4 and P5 provide the strongest target-level support. The principal network-wide limitation is that 'Surface' and 'anoxic' do not specify the conditions needed to establish an operational environmental synthesis.
